newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Spain to drop court action over EU cable TV law.
newsitem.headline: Spain to drop court action over EU cable TV law.

text.p: Spain plans to drop a court challenge to European Union rules allowing cable television networks to compete with phone monopolies in a sign of its willingness to deregulate its telecoms market, EU sources said.

The sources said Spanish Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado pledged on Wednesday to withdraw its complaint asking the European Court of Justice to annul the rules, which took effect in January.
Spain is under strong pressure to open its market to free competition from January 1, 1998 -- the date agreed by all but a few smaller EU states.

The Commission is using its power to review the Unisource telecoms alliance between partly state-controlled Telefonica de Espana, Telia AB of Sweden, Dutch PTT and Swiss PTT as leverage. Another trump is a joint venture between Unisource and U.S. telecoms operator AT&T called Uniworld, which was also submitted for EU clearance.
The January 1996 rules allow cable TV operators to offer services in the telecoms sectors already deregulated such as home banking and mobile communications.
The rules, adopted by the Commission alone under special EU treaty powers, also require governments to abolish restrictions on "interconnections" between cable TV and public telecoms networks.

Although the withdrawal of the court action will help the Spanish case, the essential condition remained that Madrid must allow fair and effective competition in its telecoms market from 1998 or shortly after, a Commission source said.

At a meeting in Brussels on Wednesday with European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, Arias Salgado confirmed that Spain would renounce its controversial option to delay liberalising its telecoms market by five years, the sources said.

But they said its offer to adhere to the 1998 deadline was not acceptable to Van Miert because it was not willing to bring in effective competition by actually granting licenses until the following year.
